title: Start Strong: Five Classroom Foundations That Pay Off All Year
author: Jamie Lee Clark
summary: Writing for the DistillED newsletter, Jamie Lee Clark argues that a strong classroom culture is not a matter of teacher charisma or a one-off expectations talk but a set of five explicitly taught, rehearsed routines: entry routine, attention signal, consistent lesson shape, early engineered success, and paired-talk with accountability. The central mechanism is working memory: any routine left unset forces students to spend cognitive resources figuring out logistics rather than thinking about content, and that cost recurs every single lesson until the routine is automatic. Clark draws on Peps McCrea's account of motivation as an ongoing cost-value calculation and on Barak Rosenshine's Principles of Instruction, particularly the 80-percent success-rate benchmark and the review-first lesson structure, to argue that these routines are not classroom-management tricks but load-bearing infrastructure for learning itself. The piece frames the five foundations as an interlocking system rather than a checklist, since each earlier routine makes the next one easier to establish, and insists they must be revisited across the year, not just taught once in September, because unpractised routines decay like any other skill.
points: Clark's working-memory argument reframes classroom routines as a cognitive-load issue, not a discipline issue: every foundation left unset is something students must consciously work out mid-lesson, competing directly with capacity available for the actual content.

The piece explicitly rejects the common failure mode of a single September expectations talk, citing that an unrehearsed routine 'fades within a fortnight' and must be re-taught like content, not merely announced.

Drawing on Peps McCrea, Clark frames student motivation as a live value-expectancy-cost calculation, meaning unpredictable routines cause disengagement that looks like defiance but is actually a rational withdrawal of effort.

Rosenshine's 80-percent success-rate principle is used to justify keeping content difficulty high while lowering the stakes of early attempts (mini-whiteboards, verbal rehearsal) rather than diluting the curriculum itself.

The five foundations are presented as sequentially interdependent, an attention signal is far weaker without an already-secure entry routine, and paired talk fails without the confidence built by earlier engineered successes, arguing against picking foundations à la carte.
quotes: A strong start is the deliberate, explicit teaching of five foundational routines that help make your classroom run like clockwork.
A new class that spends September unsure of what to do spends the rest of the year paying that tax in lost attention and disrupted learning.
Working memory is limited, and it doesn't distinguish between "productive thinking about your lesson" and "working out where to sit, whether it's safe to answer, and what happens if I get this wrong.
A class that doesn't yet trust the routines, doesn't know whether participation is safe, and can't predict what's coming next is a class whose motivation system is quietly voting to disengage.
A success rate of 80 percent shows that students are learning the material, and it also shows that the students are challenged." — Barak Rosenshine, Principles of Instruction (2012)
A routine taught once in September and never revisited decays exactly the way any other unpractised skill does.

An attention signal is far less useful without an entry routine that's already secured a calm start. Paired talk only works if early tasks have already built enough confidence that students have something worth saying to a partner.
Get these five running by the end of the first fortnight, and you've removed five recurring taxes on attention that would otherwise be quietly charged every lesson until July.
